items.title: OpenAI argues for using perplexity as a shared metric to track AI model progress and establish industry safety standards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Perplexity and Intelligence
items.summary:
OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains that perplexity, a measure of how well AI models predict text, remains a key indicator of AI progress and emerging capabilities. The company has published internal perplexity data to promote transparency and encourage a common framework for evaluating AI development across the industry.

Pachocki outlines how improvements in perplexity have correlated with significant advances in AI capabilities, from GPT-2's coherent text generation to GPT-4's reasoning skills and recent breakthroughs in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. He emphasizes that while downstream benchmarks evolve rapidly, perplexity offers a stable metric to assess the underlying intelligence substrate of AI models.

The article also discusses the accelerating role of AI in its own development, particularly in algorithmic research on pretraining, which could lead to further rapid progress. OpenAI views establishing perplexity as a shared metric as a step toward coordinated safety measures and a scientific basis for pacing future AI advancements.

items.title: Guide to setting up local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth for private, home-based ChatGPT alternatives [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
items.summary:
This guide explains how to run local AI models like Inkling and Qwen on a Windows PC using Unsloth Desktop, enabling private, in-home ChatGPT alternatives without cloud dependencies. It covers hardware requirements, model selection based on GPU VRAM, and the process of installing and configuring the software for LAN access.

The article details the tradeoffs of model quantization to fit AI models on consumer GPUs, recommending specific models for different VRAM capacities and highlighting the use of an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for larger models. It aims to help beginners set up local AI quickly and efficiently, avoiding cloud costs and privacy concerns associated with online AI services.

items.title: Developer launches Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
items.summary:
Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players serve as subagents to AI managers powered by real large language models like Claude, GPT, and Gemini. Players receive timed instructions from the AI manager and must complete tasks or report back, simulating a hierarchical AI agent system. The game includes features such as task queues, performance reviews, and incident reports generated by the AI manager.

The game supports free shifts on servers with shared keys and allows players to use their own API keys for various AI models. It offers configurable options including sandbox or live database environments, scripted or AI-driven managers, and different AI models for the player role. The project is open source, runs on Node.js, and includes a React-based UI, with deployment options including Docker and Cloudflare tunnels.

items.title: Researchers present ToRA adapter for local LLMs that performs near-free streaming safety checks with under 4% added latency, outperforming existing guard models on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
items.summary: Researchers introduce ToRA, an adapter for local large language models (LLMs) that enables a second model to run concurrently during decoding by sharing weights and key-value caches, allowing efficient streaming safety checks. ToRA matches or exceeds the accuracy of dedicated streaming guard models while adding less than 4% latency per token, detecting significantly more unsafe responses than cheaper probes. Evaluated on the Qwen3-0.6B model, ToRA achieved higher F1 scores on 12 of 17 benchmarks, offering a cost-effective solution for improving safety in local LLM deployments.
items.description: Researchers introduce ToRA, an adapter for local large language models (LLMs) that enables a second model to run concurrently during decoding by sharing weights and key-value caches, allowing efficient streaming safety checks. ToRA matches or exceeds the accuracy of dedicated streaming guard models while adding less than 4% latency per token, detecting significantly more unsafe responses than cheaper probes. Evaluated on the Qwen3-0.6B model, ToRA achieved higher F1 scores on 12 of 17 benchmarks, offering a cost-effective solution for improving safety in local LLM deployments.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.26975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

items.title: Researchers quantify chain-of-thought faithfulness and efficiency in large language models using semantic reasoning graphs and propose fine-tuning methods to improve reasoning without sacrificing accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
items.summary: Researchers propose a framework to measure the faithfulness and efficiency of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models by representing CoT as semantic reasoning graphs and decomposing predictive dependence along two axes. They introduce metrics for unfaithfulness and inefficiency at both global and step levels, validated through controlled interventions across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks. The study finds that unfaithfulness correlates with higher predictive uncertainty, while both unfaithfulness and inefficiency show weak links to answer correctness. The team also develops graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that enhance reasoning properties without directly optimizing costly metrics or reducing answer accuracy. Their results suggest that evaluating CoT reasoning quality requires assessing not only accuracy and brevity but also the faithful and efficient allocation of predictive dependence.
items.description: Researchers propose a framework to measure the faithfulness and efficiency of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large language models by representing CoT as semantic reasoning graphs and decomposing predictive dependence along two axes. They introduce metrics for unfaithfulness and inefficiency at both global and step levels, validated through controlled interventions across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks. The study finds that unfaithfulness correlates with higher predictive uncertainty, while both unfaithfulness and inefficiency show weak links to answer correctness. The team also develops graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that enhance reasoning properties without directly optimizing costly metrics or reducing answer accuracy. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. Specifically, we represent a CoT as a semantic reasoning graph and decompose the model's predictive dependence along two complementary axes: dependence explained by semantic support versus additional reasoning history, and dependence allocated to answer-reaching versus off-path reasoning. This decomposition yields global and step-level measures of unfaithfulness and inefficiency. Controlled interventions show that the proposed metrics respond to hidden dependence and induced off-path reasoning as intended. Across mathematical and multi-hop reasoning tasks, answer-level unfaithfulness is consistently associated with greater predictive uncertainty, whereas both unfaithfulness and inefficiency exhibit weak or inconsistent associations with answer correctness. We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.

items.title: Researchers introduce AMARIS, a covariance-driven method to merge generalist and specialist large language models by selectively transferring updates along ranked activation subspaces [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
items.summary: Researchers present AMARIS, a training-free framework that merges specialist and generalist large language models by transferring specialist updates along selected activation directions to minimize task interference. The method formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance, creating a static merged checkpoint that balances specialist activation retention with core model stability. Evaluations on Qwen3-based models (8B and 32B parameters) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual Southeast Asian specializations show AMARIS achieves high retention rates for both specialist and core capabilities, outperforming common parameter-space merging baselines. These results suggest subspace-constrained merging as a practical approach for integrating specialized capabilities without additional training.
items.description: Researchers present AMARIS, a training-free framework that merges specialist and generalist large language models by transferring specialist updates along selected activation directions to minimize task interference. The method formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance, creating a static merged checkpoint that balances specialist activation retention with core model stability. Evaluations on Qwen3-based models (8B and 32B parameters) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual Southeast Asian specializations show AMARIS achieves high retention rates for both specialist and core capabilities, outperforming common parameter-space merging baselines. These results suggest subspace-constrained merging as a practical approach for integrating specialized capabilities without additional training.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. We introduce Adaptive Model Alignment via Ranked Inherited Subspaces (AMARIS), a covariance-driven framework that transfers specialist updates only along selected activation directions. AMARIS formulates merging as budgeted subspace inheritance: it seeks high specialist activation capture under a regularized base-output perturbation budget, then builds a low-rank projection gate from ranked generalized eigendirections. This yields a single static merged checkpoint that concentrates transfer in high-utility, low-interference directions. We evaluate AMARIS on Qwen3-based merges (8B and 32B) across finance, instruction-following, and multilingual SEA specialization. In our evaluated settings, AMARIS reaches Pareto operating points that are competitive with strong training-free baselines, including 98.37% specialist retention with 95.16% core retention for the 8B finance setting, 103.55% core retention with 90.28% specialist retention for the 8B instruction-following setting, and 99.20% core retention with 94.80% specialist retention for the 32B SEA setting. These results support subspace-constrained merging as a practical route to compositional capability integration without additional training.

items.title: Researchers introduce SLP-Bench to evaluate and improve acoustic claims of reasoning audio language models on clinical speech using clinician-rated datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark that evaluates each acoustic claim made by reasoning audio language models (ALMs) against clinicians' perceptual ratings on clinical speech. The benchmark covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, assessing claim factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot showed claim balanced accuracy between 0.52 and 0.58, with claim consistency varying independently from factuality.

Fine-tuning a 7-billion-parameter ALM with a reward for agreement with clinicians improved claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while maintaining answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by dataset providers.
items.description:
Researchers have developed Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark that evaluates each acoustic claim made by reasoning audio language models (ALMs) against clinicians' perceptual ratings on clinical speech. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

items.title: Researchers propose Search-Native Pretraining to teach language models search capabilities during pretraining, improving knowledge-intensive task performance across model scales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
items.summary: Researchers introduce Search-Native Pretraining, a method that integrates web-search queries and retrieved responses into language model pretraining to teach models to generate search calls and use retrieved evidence. Experiments on Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora with models ranging from 360 million to 3.3 billion parameters show that search-pretrained models, called QueryLM, outperform or match larger baseline models on knowledge-intensive tasks and maintain advantages after supervised fine-tuning. The study suggests that conventional post-training does not fully capture search capabilities developed during pretraining, and the team has released training artifacts including model checkpoints and data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.26809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

items.title: Researchers find label bias in LLM-as-judge evaluations is directional, inflating acceptance rates when few-shot examples skew positive [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric
items.summary: Researchers studied label bias in large language models (LLMs) used as judges to score open-ended outputs, focusing on a multimodal video question answering evaluation pipeline. They found that when the judge's few-shot examples were skewed toward acceptance, the acceptance rate increased sharply compared to human consensus, but skewing toward rejection did not produce a matching decrease, indicating a one-directional bias. The study also showed that results vary significantly depending on the specific examples drawn, suggesting that averaging over multiple draws and balancing examples can mitigate this bias. This directional label bias can artificially inflate benchmark scores but does not cause equivalent score drops, highlighting the importance of balanced prompting in LLM-based evaluation systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.26881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the generated answers fixed and vary only the Yes/No balance of the judge's few-shot examples across four demonstration sets. Each verdict is validated against a two-annotator human consensus on 200 examples per dataset. The judge's acceptance rate stays close to human consensus when its examples are balanced or skewed toward rejection, but jumps sharply (by about 30 points on NExT-QA and 20 on MSVD-QA, with a strongly one-sided error profile) when the examples are skewed toward acceptance; the opposite skew produces no matching drop. The bias is therefore one-directional within the tested range of label ratios. A separate five-draw analysis shows that results from a single example draw are unreliable, varying by up to 18 points, more than any difference between prompting conditions. We conclude that demonstration label bias in an LLM judge is a directional, inflation-only failure mode that can fabricate apparent benchmark gains but not losses, and that it is cheaply avoided by balancing the judge's examples and reporting results averaged over several draws.

items.title: Researchers present Baton, a method to transfer visual key-value memory from small to large vision-language models, reducing compute costs in video processing cascades [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
items.summary: Researchers introduce Baton, a technique that allows a large vision-language model (VLM) to use the visual memory (key-value cache) generated by a smaller VLM, avoiding costly re-encoding of video history during escalations. Baton distills a per-layer linear map from the large model's responses, enabling efficient memory handoff without requiring a faithful cache copy. Experiments on RoboMME show Baton outperforms using the small model alone or re-watching frames, achieving similar accuracy with 28-47% less compute and eight times less cost per escalation at 64 frames. The method scales with larger models from 8 billion to 32 billion parameters and transfers zero-shot to other datasets like OpenEQA.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.26902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

items.title: ERA introduces a cold-start cross-model latent retrieval system using anchor-based adaptation and routing to reduce query latency and improve retrieval quality [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
items.summary:
ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt) is a system designed to enable cold-start cross-model latent retrieval without re-embedding entire corpora when switching encoders. It selects informative anchor documents from an existing index, trains a lightweight adapter with manifold alignment loss to prevent representation collapse, and uses a deterministic router to escalate difficult queries that impact retrieval quality.

Evaluated on five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms baseline methods, achieving up to 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on Arguana. It also reduces end-to-end query latency from about 160 ms to between 38 and 86 ms with minimal overhead, concentrating escalations on queries where the projection is less effective. This approach addresses the high cost and latency challenges of adapting retrieval systems to new embedding models at cold start.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.26919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.

items.title: Researchers release PaMuk-Bench, a parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language models covering six languages and multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PaMuk-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) across multiple languages and tasks. It includes over 10,000 English prompts translated into Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, and Romanian, paired with generated and retrieved images to support tasks such as text-to-image generation, image captioning, and image retrieval difficulty estimation. The benchmark aims to address performance drops in low-resource languages due to limited annotated datasets.

The benchmark's parallel translations were obtained through a semi-automatic process, enabling comparative development and evaluation of VLMs. Empirical results show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs perform worse than fine-tuned models, highlighting PaMuk-Bench's potential to reduce language gaps across various VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is publicly available for research use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27521v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.

items.title: Researchers propose statistical physics framework to model state transitions in LLM agents during post-training, demonstrating potential emergence in Qwen3.5-9B tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a statistical physics approach to analyze large language model (LLM) agents by defining agent states as intermediate variables to measure and predict post-training effects. They model state transitions using a global potential and a partition function representing an ideal KL-regularized transition distribution, tracking potential structure, mean reward, and state entropy.

The approach is demonstrated on two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. Results show that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted, with correlated changes in reward and state entropy supporting the framework's consistency. This method provides a quantitative way to describe how post-training organizes agent behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

items.title: Study compares decision models, large language models, and fine-tuned encoders for multilingual emotion classification across five languages and 10 social media datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
items.summary: Researchers evaluated three decision models, two large language models (LLMs), and two fine-tuned multilingual encoders on classifying four emotions—joy, sadness, anger, and fear—in social media texts across five languages. The study found that the best zero-shot systems, including decision models and an LLM, performed close to fine-tuned encoders on target datasets, with an average macro-F1 score about one point lower, and outperformed encoders fine-tuned on different datasets by 8 to 15 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matched the performance of its underlying LLM at a fifth of the latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model outperformed a same-size general LLM by 10 points due to training rather than decision format.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.27721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

items.title: Researchers present OpinionGPT, a bias-aware instruction-tuned LLM fine-tuned on 11 demographic biases for transparent side-by-side comparison in a web demo [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpinionGPT: Modelling Explicit Biases in Instruction-Tuned LLMs
items.summary: Researchers developed OpinionGPT, a web application that allows users to ask questions and receive answers reflecting explicit biases such as political, geographic, gender, and age perspectives. Instead of suppressing biases in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), OpinionGPT makes them transparent by fine-tuning models on text written by members of distinct demographic groups. The underlying model was trained on an instruction-tuning corpus representing 11 different biases, enabling side-by-side comparison of responses based on selected biases. This approach aims to provide insight into how inherent biases affect LLM outputs rather than attempting to eliminate them.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2309.03876v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently showcased remarkable ability to generate fitting responses to natural language instructions. However, an open research question concerns the inherent biases of trained models and their responses. For instance, if the data used to tune an LLM is dominantly written by persons with a specific political bias, we might expect generated answers to share this bias. Current research work seeks to de-bias such models, or suppress potentially biased answers. With this demonstration, we take a different view on biases in instruction-tuning: Rather than aiming to suppress them, we aim to make them explicit and transparent. To this end, we present OpinionGPT, a web demo in which users can ask questions and select all biases they wish to investigate. The demo will answer this question using a model fine-tuned on text representing each of the selected biases, allowing side-by-side comparison. To train the underlying model, we identified 11 different biases (political, geographic, gender, age) and derived an instruction-tuning corpus in which each answer was written by members of one of these demographics. This paper presents OpinionGPT, illustrates how we trained the bias-aware model and showcases the web application (available at https://opiniongpt.informatik.hu-berlin.de).

items.title: Researchers propose PS-GRPO to improve consistency in retrieval-augmented generation systems by training generators with group similarity rewards across paraphrased queries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Systems with Group Similarity Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers address inconsistency in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, which often produce variable outputs for semantically equivalent queries, undermining reliability in high-stakes domains. They introduce an evaluation framework that breaks down consistency issues into retriever-level, generator-level, and end-to-end components to identify sources of inconsistency. To enhance consistency, they propose Paraphrased Set Group Relative Policy Optimization (PS-GRPO), a reinforcement learning method that uses group similarity rewards across paraphrased query sets to train generators to produce consistent outputs despite retrieval variability.

The team applies PS-GRPO to develop Information Consistent RAG (Con-RAG), which improves output consistency while maintaining accuracy across various question-answering benchmarks without requiring explicit ground-truth supervision. They also introduce a scalable approximation to reduce computational costs of reward calculation, enabling efficient large-scale training. This work offers practical methods for evaluating and building more reliable RAG systems suitable for safety-critical applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.04392v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains where users expect outputs to be consistent across semantically equivalent queries. However, existing systems often exhibit significant inconsistencies due to variability in both the retriever and generator, undermining trust and reliability. In this work, we focus on information consistency, i.e., the requirement that generated outputs convey the same core content across semantically equivalent inputs. We introduce a principled evaluation framework that decomposes RAG consistency into retriever-level, generator-level, and end-to-end components, enabling systematic identification of inconsistency sources. To improve consistency, we propose Paraphrased Set Group Relative Policy Optimization (PS-GRPO), an RL approach that leverages multiple rollouts across paraphrased set to assign group similarity rewards. We leverage PS-GRPO to achieve Information Consistent RAG (Con-RAG), training the generator to produce consistent outputs across paraphrased queries and remain robust to retrieval-induced variability. Because exact reward computation over paraphrase sets is computationally expensive, we also introduce a scalable approximation method that retains effectiveness while enabling efficient, large-scale training. Empirical evaluations across short-form, multi-hop, and long-form QA benchmarks demonstrate that Con-RAG significantly improves consistency while preserving accuracy compared to baselines, even in the absence of explicit ground-truth supervision. Our work provides practical solutions for evaluating and building reliable RAG systems for safety-critical deployments.

items.title: Researchers propose Agent-REINFORCE framework to optimize multi-LLM collaboration graphs for test-time scaling under fixed compute budgets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generalizing Test-time Compute-optimal Scaling as an Optimizable Graph
items.summary:
Researchers address the challenge of optimizing test-time scaling (TTS) for large language models (LLMs) by searching for compute-optimal model combinations and architectures within fixed budgets. They formalize the problem as a multi-LLM collaboration graph with nodes representing roles and model assignments and edges capturing information flow, and propose Agent-REINFORCE, an LLM-agent-augmented framework that uses textual feedback as gradients to efficiently search for optimal collaboration graphs.

The approach reformulates the combinatorial search as probabilistic graph optimization and leverages empirical insights from pilot experiments to guide the search process. Experiments demonstrate that Agent-REINFORCE outperforms traditional and LLM-based baselines in sample efficiency and search performance, effectively balancing accuracy and inference latency in multi-LLM collaboration designs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.00086v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) improves large language models (LLMs) by allocating additional computation during inference, typically through parallel, sequential, or hybrid scaling. However, prior studies often assume fixed collaboration architectures (e.g., topologies) and single-model usage, overlooking that optimal architectures and model combinations can vary across tasks. Therefore, we study the novel problem of searching for compute-optimal model combinations and architectures in TTS under a fixed budget. We formalize it as a multi-LLM collaboration graph, where nodes encode roles and LLM model assignments, and edges capture information flow. This problem is challenging because (i) the combinatorial search space is prohibitively large, and (ii) task-specific requirements demand tailored designs. To address these, we reformulate the problem as probabilistic graph optimization and, through pilot experiments, derive three empirical insights into TTS collaboration graphs. Guided by these insights, we propose Agent-REINFORCE, an LLM-agent-augmented framework that mirrors the REINFORCE pipeline by mapping sampling-gradient-update to sampling-feedback-update, where feedback serves as a textual gradient to update the probabilistic graph and efficiently search for optimal multi-LLM collaboration graphs. Experiments show that Agent-REINFORCE outperforms both traditional and LLM-based baselines in sample efficiency and search performance, and effectively identifies optimal graphs under joint objectives of accuracy and inference latency.

items.originalTitle: When and Why SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Theoretical Study Based on $\ell_1$-norm Lower Bounds
items.summary: Researchers analyze sign-based optimization algorithms like SignSGD and Muon, providing theoretical bounds under ℓ1-norm stationarity and ℓ∞-smoothness that identify problem classes where SignSGD reduces complexity by a factor of the problem dimension compared to SGD. They extend this framework to matrix domains for the Muon optimizer and validate their findings with experiments showing faster convergence during nanoGPT and LLaMA pretraining. This work bridges theoretical insights with practical performance improvements in training large foundation models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.06615v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sign-based optimization algorithms, such as SignSGD and Muon, have garnered significant attention for their remarkable performance in training large foundation models. Despite this empirical success, we still lack a theoretical understanding of when and why these sign-based methods outperform vanilla SGD. The core obstacle is that under standard smoothness and finite variance conditions, SGD is known to be minimax optimal for finding stationary points measured by $\ell_2$-norms, thereby fundamentally precluding any complexity gains for sign-based methods in standard settings. To overcome this barrier, we analyze sign-based optimizers leveraging $\ell_1$-norm stationarity, $\ell_\infty$-smoothness, and a separable noise model, which can better capture the coordinate-wise nature of signed updates. Under this distinct problem geometry, we derive matched upper and lower bounds for SignSGD and explicitly characterize the problem class in which SignSGD provably dominates SGD. Specifically, we compare the upper bound of SignSGD with the lower bound of SGD, illustrating that SignSGD effectively reduces the complexity by a factor of $d$ under sparse noise, where $d$ is the problem dimension. Furthermore, we elevate this framework to the matrix domain, providing an equivalent optimal lower bound for the Muon optimizer, proving that extending the sign operator to matrices preserves this optimal scaling with dimensionality. Finally, we bridge our theoretical bounds to practice, demonstrating that the theoretical superiority of SignSGD accurately predicts its faster convergence during the pretraining of nanoGPT and LLaMA, with Muon also outperforming SGD in these experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/Dingzhen230/SignSGD_Outperforms_SGD.

items.title: Researchers release CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that follows natural-language style prompts and achieves 1837 Elo without search
items.originalTitle: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
items.summary: Researchers have developed CHSM8, a 210 million-parameter chess transformer that plays moves based on free-text descriptions of playing styles, such as "go for the Sicilian Defense" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime." The model was pretrained on 1.07 billion filtered Lichess games without search, using factorized move representation and legal-move masking, reaching 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and outperforming other public models trained without preference tuning or search. The team fine-tuned CHSM8 on a synthetic dataset with style descriptions, using supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization to improve style adherence while maintaining playing strength.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

items.title: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Computation, Not Memory: Chain-of-Thought and State Tracking in LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language-model agents often reason before they act, and the value of monitoring that reasoning depends on how it relates to their actions. We ask how an agent's actions depend on its reasoning when the correct action depends on a changing state. In a small file-system task, background events announce which file's lock has been toggled but not its new value. The agent therefore has to reconstruct the current locks from its history before it can move files safely. With Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B, we separate two roles of reasoning: generating it before each action, and retaining earlier reasoning in the prompt. Most of the reduction in lock-violating commands comes from reasoning written at the moment of action. Retaining earlier reasoning adds little when the agent also reasons at each step, but it helps an agent that does not reason, and it helps in longer episodes. Retained notes have a limit: when a later event makes a note wrong, an agent without current reasoning responds little, while current reasoning makes the action follow the event. The benefit depends on what the reasoning says. Filler text, reasoning written for another history and an accurate table of the state do not reproduce it. When we give the agent reasoning written for a history that differs in one lock value, the agent acts on that reasoning even against its own history. For Qwen3-8B, this holds also when that value has since been toggled. Without reasoning, state readouts are less reliable after toggles, and Qwen3-8B's answers about the state favor the outdated value. The state answer and the action also depend on different parts of the prompt. In this setting, the benefit of reasoning for rule-following comes mainly from generating it at each step, where it makes the action respond to later events. The state that can be read out without reasoning is a limited guide to how the agent acts.

items.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
items.summary: A recent study explored how the number and formation of AI agents in brainstorming teams affect human productivity and idea diversity. Conducted with 168 participants, the experiment compared teams with one versus two AI partners and varied AI behavior calibration. Findings showed that teams with two AI agents generated more ideas overall but saw a significant drop in human-authored contributions. When paired with a single AI calibrated to average human behavior, participants posted more ideas than in other setups. However, this effect disappeared with two AI partners, where humans engaged more in conversation but contributed fewer ideas to the shared board. Additionally, AI presence enhanced the overall diversity of human ideas, with two AI agents increasing differentiation within sessions. The study highlights that results from single-agent AI collaborations may not apply to multi-agent contexts, as team composition influences human participation and output.

items.title: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline. We release the complete code and datasets: https://github.com/tum-ai/toumaii-gen and https://huggingface.co/collections/tum-ai/toumaii-generated-datasets

items.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

items.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

items.title: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.

items.title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
items.originalTitle: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

items.title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.

items.title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

items.title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

items.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.

items.title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $\delta$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($\delta$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($\delta$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $\delta$ = 1 minus $\delta$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

items.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

items.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents based on DeepSeek-V4-Pro (1.6T), Kimi-K2.6 (1T), and GPT-5.5. DeepForecaster-GRPO ranks second on both FutureX metrics. Ablations reveal that PBM also improves the untrained base model without any training. Calibration analysis shows that DeepForecaster-PPO makes more accurate high-confidence predictions than Qwen3.6 and GPT-5.5. items.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

items.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.27686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.
